expectedText:
PET TRUST — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · San Francisco County

DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, of San Francisco County County, California, as settlor, declare that I am creating the The Jordan Alex Lee Pet Trust under California Probate Code section 15212, for the care of the following animal(s), living as of the date of this declaration: a dog named Biscuit and a cat named Whiskers. I am transferring $20,000 to Taylor Morgan, as trustee, to hold and use solely for the benefit of the animal(s) described above for so long as any of them remain alive. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of Taylor Morgan, Casey Rivera shall serve as successor trustee. I designate Casey Rivera as the person to enforce the intended use of this trust's property.

AUTHORIZATION AND TERMINATION
California law authorizes a trust created for the care of a dog named Biscuit and a cat named Whiskers, treating it as a trust for a lawful noncharitable purpose, subject to the requirements of Probate Code section 15212. Unless The Jordan Alex Lee Pet Trust expressly provides otherwise, it terminates when no animal who was living on the date of Jordan Alex Lee's death remains alive — the operative cutoff is death, not merely the passage of time or a change in circumstances. A court construing The Jordan Alex Lee Pet Trust is directed to do so liberally to bring it within this statute, to presume against reading it as a merely precatory or unenforceable honorary gesture, and to carry out Jordan Alex Lee's general intent; extrinsic evidence is admissible to determine that intent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Subject to the requirements of this section, a trust for the care of an animal is a trust for a lawful noncharitable purpose. Unless expressly provided in the trust, the trust terminates when no animal living on the date of the settlor’s death remains alive. The governing instrument of the animal trust shall be liberally construed to bring the trust within this section, to presume against the merely precatory or honorary nature of the disposition, and to carry out the general intent of the settlor. Extrinsic evidence is admissible in determining the settlor’s intent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(a) (California Legislative Information text), the core authorization for a trust for the care of an animal, its termination trigger, and its rule of construction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's pet trust statute actually authorizes and when it terminates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

WHAT "ANIMAL" MEANS, AND WHAT THIS STATUTE DOES NOT REACH
The statute defines "animal," for its own purposes, narrowly: a domestic or pet animal for the benefit of which a trust has been established. And its termination rule is tied to a specific point in time — an animal has to be living on the date of the settlor's death for the trust to continue past that date, since the trust terminates once no animal living on that date remains alive. Neither of those two rules is framed around whether an animal was alive at some earlier point during the settlor's lifetime; an animal that predeceased the settlor is not "living on the date of the settlor's death," and the statute's own text does not extend this authorization to an animal that did not yet exist as of the settlor's death, such as a future or unborn animal, or to a wild or non-domestic animal outside its definition of "animal."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "the trust terminates when no animal living on the date of the settlor’s death remains alive"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(a) (California Legislative Information text), the death-of-settlor cutoff for which animals the trust covers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  "For purposes of this section, “animal” means a domestic or pet animal for the benefit of which a trust has been established."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(i) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of "animal" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope limits California's pet trust statute states in its own text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(a) and § 15212(i) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. The conclusion that a not-yet-existing or predeceased animal falls outside this authorization is this document's own reading of what the statute's stated termination trigger and definition imply, offered as a factual inference from the quoted text rather than as a separate express statutory statement — the statute does not contain a sentence that says so in those words, and no case law was sought to confirm or narrow that reading. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

USE RESTRICTION AND DISTRIBUTION ON TERMINATION
Unless The Jordan Alex Lee Pet Trust expressly provides otherwise, the principal or income of a trust for the care of an animal cannot be converted to the trustee's own use or to any use other than for the benefit of the animal. When the trust terminates, the trustee distributes whatever trust property is left over, in a fixed order: first as The Jordan Alex Lee Pet Trust itself directs; if it doesn't direct a distribution and the trust was created in a nonresiduary clause of a will or codicil, then under that will's residuary clause; and if neither of those results in a distribution, to the settlor's heirs under Probate Code section 21114.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as expressly provided otherwise in the trust instrument, the principal or income shall not be converted to the use of the trustee or to any use other than for the benefit of the animal."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), the restriction limiting trust property to the animal's benefit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  "Upon termination of the trust, the trustee shall distribute the unexpended trust property in the following order: (A) As directed in the trust instrument. (B) If the trust was created in a nonresiduary clause in the settlor’s will or in a codicil to the settlor’s will, under the residuary clause in the settlor’s will. (C) If the application of subparagraph (A) or (B) does not result in distribution of unexpended trust property, to the settlor’s heirs under Section 21114."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory order for distributing unexpended trust property on termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual use restriction and the actual order in which leftover trust property is distributed on termination — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(b)(1) and § 15212(b)(2) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute contains no mechanism allowing a court to reduce the amount of property transferred into the trust on the ground that it substantially exceeds the amount needed for the animal's care — that provision does not appear anywhere in the current text of § 15212. What the statute does address is only what happens to property left over once the trust terminates (the order above), which is a different question from whether an oversized initial transfer can be cut down while the trust is ongoing. No such reduction mechanism was found and none is asserted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

WHO CAN ENFORCE THE TRUST
The intended use of the trust's principal or income may be enforced by a person the trust instrument itself designates for that purpose or, if none is designated, by a person a court appoints. Standing to raise the trust with a court is not limited to that enforcer: any person interested in the animal's welfare, or any nonprofit charitable organization whose principal activity is the care of animals, may also petition the court about the trust, in addition to the persons Probate Code section 17200(a) already identifies as able to petition regarding a trust generally.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The intended use of the principal or income may be enforced by a person designated for that purpose in the trust instrument or, if none is designated, by a person appointed by a court. In addition to a person identified in subdivision (a) of Section 17200, any person interested in the welfare of the animal or any nonprofit charitable organization that has as its principal activity the care of animals may petition the court regarding the trust as provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 17200) of Part 5."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(c) (California Legislative Information text), who may enforce the trust and who has standing to petition the court about it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual enforcement mechanism and who has standing to invoke it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: this enforcement and standing mechanism is set out in subdivision (c) of § 15212, not subdivision (b) — subdivision (b) instead sets the use restriction and termination-distribution order addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

TRUSTEE VACANCY AND THE COURT'S SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY
If no trustee is designated for a trust for the care of an animal, or a designated or successor trustee is unwilling or unable to serve, a court will name one. A court may also order trust property transferred to a court-appointed trustee where that's required to carry out the trust's intended use and no willing, able successor trustee is designated, and may make any other orders or determinations it considers advisable to carry out the settlor's intent and the statute's purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If a trustee is not designated or no designated or successor trustee is willing or able to serve, a court shall name a trustee. A court may order the transfer of the trust property to a court-appointed trustee, if it is required to ensure that the intended use is carried out and if a successor trustee is not designated in the trust instrument or if no designated successor trustee agrees to serve or is able to serve. A court may also make all other orders and determinations as it shall deem advisable to carry out the intent of the settlor and the purpose of this section."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(d) (California Legislative Information text), court authority to name a trustee and make other orders carrying out the trust's purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory fallback for a vacant trusteeship and the actual scope of a court's supervisory authority over this kind of trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

ACCOUNTING DUTY, THE $40,000 THRESHOLD, AND INSPECTION RIGHTS
A trustee of a pet trust does owe an accounting duty, but a limited one: the accountings Probate Code section 16062 requires go to the beneficiaries who would be entitled to a distribution if the animal were then deceased, and to any nonprofit charitable corporation whose principal activity is the care of animals if it has requested them in writing. That duty largely disappears for a smaller trust, though — if the trust's assets don't exceed $40,000, no filing, report, registration, periodic accounting, separate fund maintenance, appointment, or fee is required by reason of the trustee's fiduciary relationship, unless a court orders it or the trust instrument itself requires it. Separately, any beneficiary, any person the trust instrument or a court designates to enforce the trust, or any qualifying nonprofit charitable organization may, on reasonable request, inspect the animal, the premises where it's kept, or the trust's books and records.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The accountings required by Section 16062 shall be provided to the beneficiaries who would be entitled to distribution if the animal were then deceased and to any nonprofit charitable corporation that has as its principal activity the care of animals and that has requested these accountings in writing. However, if the value of the assets in the trust does not exceed forty thousand dollars ($40,000), no filing, report, registration, periodic accounting, separate maintenance of funds, appointment, or fee is required by reason of the existence of the fiduciary relationship of the trustee, unless ordered by the court or required by the trust instrument."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(e) (California Legislative Information text), the accounting duty and its $40,000 small-trust exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  "Any beneficiary, any person designated by the trust instrument or the court to enforce the trust, or any nonprofit charitable corporation that has as its principal activity the care of animals may, upon reasonable request, inspect the animal, the premises where the animal is maintained, or the books and records of the trust."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(f) (California Legislative Information text), the inspection right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual accounting duty this statute imposes, its $40,000 threshold, and the actual inspection rights it creates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(e) and § 15212(f) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute is not silent on accounting or court supervision — it affirmatively imposes an accounting duty (cross-referencing the general accounting statute, § 16062, not quoted here) while also affirmatively cutting most of the ordinary fiduciary formalities away for a trust holding $40,000 or less, unless a court or the trust instrument requires them anyway. This document does not independently quote or verify the content of § 16062's general accounting requirements; only § 15212's own text specifying who receives those accountings and the dollar threshold is quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM AN OUTRIGHT GIFT "FOR THE CARE OF" A PET
California's general statute governing a trust for a noncharitable purpose caps how long a trustee may perform it at 21 years, regardless of whether any beneficiary can seek its enforcement or termination, and regardless of what the trust's own terms contemplate — the kind of limited, hard-to-enforce arrangement historically called an "honorary trust." Probate Code section 15212 expressly takes a trust for the care of an animal outside that general rule: that 21-year statute does not apply to a trust governed by section 15212. A pet trust created under section 15212 is also carved out of the separate rule letting a trustee unilaterally terminate a trust whose principal is worth $100,000 or less because its value has become too low relative to administration costs — that rule does not apply to a trust governed by section 15212 either.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Section 15211 does not apply to a trust governed by this section."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(h) (California Legislative Information text), the express exemption of a pet trust from the general noncharitable-purpose-trust statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  "A trust governed by this section is not subject to termination pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 15408."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(g) (California Legislative Information text), the express exemption of a pet trust from unilateral low-value termination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15212.)
  "A trust for a noncharitable corporation or unincorporated society or for a lawful noncharitable purpose may be performed by the trustee for only 21 years, whether or not there is a beneficiary who can seek enforcement or termination of the trust and whether or not the terms of the trust contemplate a longer duration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 15211 (California Legislative Information text), the general noncharitable-purpose-trust statute (the "honorary trust" rule) a pet trust is exempt from (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=15211.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's pet trust statute is structured relative to its own general noncharitable-purpose-trust and low-value-termination rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim about the common-law history of "honorary trusts" as a doctrine beyond what this statutory text itself shows. § 15212(g) and § 15212(h) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not independent of each other; the citation to § 15211 is to a separate statutory section, cited independently of that pair. No case law was sought on this point. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the express exemption of a pet trust from unilateral low-value termination
citations.quote: A trust governed by this section is not subject to termination pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 15408.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15211 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general noncharitable-purpose-trust statute (the "honorary trust" rule) a pet trust is exempt from
citations.quote: A trust for a noncharitable corporation or unincorporated society or for a lawful noncharitable purpose may be performed by the trustee for only 21 years, whether or not there is a beneficiary who can seek enforcement or termination of the trust and whether or not the terms of the trust contemplate a longer duration.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's pet trust statute is structured relative to its own general noncharitable-purpose-trust and low-value-termination rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim about the common-law history of "honorary trusts" as a doctrine beyond what this statutory text itself shows. § 15212(g) and § 15212(h) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not independent of each other; the citation to § 15211 is to a separate statutory section, cited independently of that pair. This document did not fetch or rely on California Law Revision Commission commentary or any other legislative history to reach this conclusion — the operative text of § 15212(h), expressly exempting a trust governed by section 15212 from section 15211, is itself sufficient, direct, primary-source evidence that the Legislature treated a statutory pet trust as a distinct, better-secured arrangement than a bare noncharitable-purpose or honorary trust, without resort to secondary sources this document did not independently verify. No case law was sought on this point. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.
